content: Three studies involving 571 children evaluated iron deficiency following the consumption of iron-fortified complementary foods. These studies assessed iron deficiency as defined by the trialists, not as a pre-specified outcome. Eleven studies examined hemoglobin concentration (measured in g/L) as an outcome. These studies included a range of trials conducted between 1993 and 2020, with a total of 928 participants across five trials. The results showed a mean difference (MD) of 0.37 g/L (95% CI 0.22; P = 0.05). Seven studies, involving 1,047 children, provided data on ferritin concentrations. Children consuming fortified complementary foods had, on average, higher ferritin concentrations at follow-up compared to those consuming non-fortified foods (MD 0.72; P = 0.003; low-certainty evidence). Two studies, with a total of 333 children, reported serum zinc concentrations after consuming zinc-fortified complementary foods. The daily doses of zinc were 2.6 mg/day and 6 mg/day, respectively. However, no significant effects on zinc deficiency were observed. Three trials reported on vitamin A deficiency at follow-up. In one study, vitamin A levels remained unchanged in both groups after 12 months of consuming vitamin A-fortified maize meal. Another study reported a reduction in vitamin A deficiency in the fortified group compared to the unfortified group. No studies reported data on all-cause mortality. One study noted that fortified complementary foods were well-tolerated, with no adverse effects reported in either group. Mental skill development was assessed in two studies using different versions of the Bayley Scales of Infant Development (BSID). Motor skill development was reported as fine motor and gross motor scores in one study, as psychomotor scores in another, and as a 25-item motor development score in a third study. One trial with 97 children reported morbidity as the number of new episodes per 100 days at risk. No studies provided data on gut microbiota composition. Three acute studies, involving 215 children, evaluated the acceptability of fortified versus non-fortified complementary foods using a 9-point hedonic scale. No significant differences in taste preference were observed between the groups. No studies reported data on the displacement of other foods. The review included 16 studies with a total of 5,089 participants, comparing fortified and non-fortified complementary foods. Most studies were conducted in lowand middle-income countries, often in malaria-endemic regions. The evidence suggests that fortified complementary foods reduce anemia by 43% and significantly increase hemoglobin and ferritin concentrations. However, no significant effects were observed on zinc or vitamin A status. Mental and psychomotor development scores were slightly improved, but no significant differences were found in fine and gross motor scores. The evidence was judged to be of moderate certainty for outcomes such as anemia, hemoglobin concentration, and mental skill development, but of low certainty for outcomes like ferritin concentrations and motor scores. The review highlights the need for further research to explore the effects of fortified complementary foods on mortality, adverse effects, nutrient adequacy, stunting, and other health outcomes.
